common.subtitle: Interactive visualizations, real-world examples, and side-by-side code comparisons. Learn the 23 GoF design patterns the modern way.
common.selectPattern: Select a pattern to start learning

concept.analogy: Imagine a country having a government. A country can have only one official government. Regardless of the personal identities of the individuals who form the government, the title, 'The Government of X', is a global point of access that identifies the group of people in charge.
concept.definition: The Singleton Pattern ensures that a class has only one instance and provides a global point of access to it.

usage.point1: Use the Singleton pattern when a class in your program should have just a single instance available to all clients; for example, a single database object shared by different parts of the program.
usage.point2: Use the Singleton pattern when you need stricter control over global variables.

demo.instructionBad: Click "New Instance" multiple times. Notice how a new object is created every time.
demo.instructionGood: Click "Get Instance" multiple times. It always returns the SAME object.

singleton.title: Singleton Pattern
singleton.description: This pattern ensures that a class, like the government in our demo, has only one official instance globally, preventing duplicate objects from being created.

concept.analogy: Imagine you are building a logistics management application. Initially, your app only handles transportation by Trucks. Later, your app becomes popular, and you need to add Ships for sea logistics.
concept.definition: If your code is tightly coupled to the Truck class, adding Ship would require changing the entire codebase. The Factory Method pattern solves this by defining an interface for creating objects in a superclass, but allowing subclasses to alter the type of objects that will be created.

usage.point1: Use the Factory Method when you don't know beforehand the exact types and dependencies of the objects your code should work with.
usage.point2: Use it when you want to provide users of your library or framework with a way to extend its internal components.
usage.point3: Use it when you want to save system resources by reusing existing objects instead of rebuilding them each time.

demo.tightCouplingDesc: Client code must import and instantiate each class directly. If product logic changes, you have to update code everywhere.
demo.factoryPatternDesc: Client just asks the Factory for a product. The creation logic is encapsulated inside the factory.

factory.title: Factory Method Pattern
factory.description: This pattern provides a way to create objects like Trucks or Ships without specifying the exact class, allowing your logistics system to introduce new transport types easily.

concept.analogy: Think of it like buying furniture. You might want a Modern Sofa and a Modern Chair. Or a Victorian Sofa and a Victorian Chair. You usually don't want to mix a Victorian Sofa with Modern Chairs. The Abstract Factory ensures you get a matching set.
concept.definition: The Abstract Factory pattern lets you produce families of related objects without specifying their concrete classes.

usage.point1: Use Abstract Factory when your code needs to work with various families of related products (e.g. Apple vs Samsung, LightTheme vs DarkTheme UI components).
usage.point2: Use it when you want to enforce that products from the same factory are used together.

demo.inconsistentFamiliesDesc: Without Abstract Factory, you might accidentally mix products that don't work well together.
demo.abstractFactoryDesc: Select a Factory. It guarantees all created products belong to the same family.
demo.warning: Warning: Incompatible ecosystems detected! AirDrop won't work!

abstractFactory.title: Abstract Factory Pattern
abstractFactory.description: This pattern lets you create families of related objects, such as a full Apple or Samsung ecosystem, ensuring all components work together harmoniously.

concept.analogy: Imagine a burger restaurant. Some customers want cheese, some want no lettuce, some want double patties. Instead of creating separate classes for CheeseBurger, NoLettuceBurger, etc., you use a builder to assemble the burger according to specific preferences.
concept.definition: The Builder pattern lets you construct complex objects step by step. The pattern allows you to produce different types and representations of an object using the same construction code.

usage.point1: Use the Builder pattern to get rid of a "telescopic constructor".
usage.point2: Use the Builder pattern when you want your code to be able to create different representations of some product (for example, stone and wooden houses).
usage.point3: Use the Builder to construct Composite trees or other complex objects.

builder.title: Builder Pattern
builder.description: This pattern helps you construct complex objects step-by-step, just like customizing a burger with specific ingredients, rather than having a rigid pre-made menu.

concept.analogy: It delegates the cloning process to the actual objects that are being cloned. The pattern declares a common interface for all objects that support cloning. This interface lets you clone an object without coupling your code to the class of that object.
concept.definition: The Prototype pattern lets you copy existing objects without making your code dependent on their classes.

usage.point1: Use the Prototype pattern when your code shouldn't depend on the concrete classes of objects that you need to copy.
usage.point2: Use the pattern when you want to reduce the number of subclasses that only differ in the way they initialize their respective objects.

demo.title: Prototype / Cloner
demo.instruction: Click the copy button on any shape to create an exact clone (Prototype). Notice how the clone inherits the properties (color, shape) of the original.

prototype.title: Prototype Pattern
prototype.description: This pattern allows you to create new objects by cloning existing ones, like copying a shape on a canvas, which is often more efficient than building from scratch.

concept.analogy: It acts as a wrapper between two objects. It catches calls for one object and transforms them to format and interface recognizable by the second object. Just like a travel power adapter converts your plug shape to fit into the foreign wall socket.
concept.definition: The Adapter pattern allows objects with incompatible interfaces to collaborate.

usage.point1: Use the Adapter class when you want to use some existing class, but its interface isn't compatible with the rest of your code.
usage.point2: Use the pattern when you want to reuse several existing subclasses that lack some common functionality that can't be added to the superclass.

adapter.title: Adapter Pattern
adapter.description: This pattern acts as a connector between incompatible interfaces, similar to how a travel adapter allows a US plug to fit into an EU socket.

concept.analogy: In the demo, the Remote (Abstraction) is separated from the Device (Implementation). You can create new types of Remotes (AdvancedRemote) without changing the Devices, and new Devices without changing the Remote code.
concept.definition: The Bridge pattern lets you split a large class or a set of closely related classes into two separate hierarchies—abstraction and implementation—which can be developed independently.

usage.point1: Use the Bridge pattern when you want to divide and organize a monolithic class that has several variants of some functionality.
usage.point2: Use the pattern when you need to extend a class in several orthogonal (independent) dimensions.

bridge.title: Bridge Pattern
bridge.description: This pattern separates an object's abstraction from its implementation, allowing you to develop remotes and devices independently, like a universal remote working with various TVs.

concept.analogy: It's perfect for hierarchical structures like file systems, menus, or organization charts. The client code can treat a simple element (File) and a complex container (Folder) in the same way (e.g., calling getSize()).
concept.definition: The Composite pattern lets you compose objects into tree structures and then work with these structures as if they were individual objects.

usage.point1: Use the Composite pattern when you want to represent part-whole hierarchies of objects.
usage.point2: Use it when you want clients to be able to ignore the difference between compositions of objects and individual objects.

demo.title: File System Tree
demo.instruction: Click any folder to calculate its total size recursively. The client treats Files and Folders uniformly.
demo.calculated: Calculated using the Composite pattern: getSize() is called recursively on all children.
demo.selectNode: Select a node to see calculation

composite.title: Composite Pattern
composite.description: This pattern lets you treat individual objects and groups of objects uniformly, like calculating the size of a single file or an entire folder of files in the same way.

concept.analogy: It's an alternative to subclassing. Instead of creating MilkCoffee, SugarCoffee, MilkSugarCoffee, you create a Coffee object and "wrap" it with MilkDecorator and then SugarDecorator.
concept.definition: The Decorator pattern lets you attach new behaviors to objects by placing these objects inside special wrapper objects that contain the behaviors.

usage.point1: Use the Decorator pattern when you need to be able to assign extra behaviors to objects at runtime without breaking the code that uses these objects.
usage.point2: Use the pattern when it's awkward or impossible to extend an object's behavior using inheritance.

decorator.title: Decorator Pattern
decorator.description: This pattern allows you to dynamically add new behaviors to an object, like adding milk or sugar to a base coffee, without altering the original code.

concept.analogy: A home theater system is complex (Amp, DVD, Projector, Screen, Lights). A Facade would be a remote with a single "Watch Movie" button that turns everything on and sets the right inputs.
concept.definition: The Facade pattern provides a simplified interface to a library, a framework, or any other complex set of classes.

usage.point1: Use the Facade pattern when you need to have a limited but straightforward interface to a complex subsystem.
usage.point2: Use the Facade when you want to structure a subsystem into layers.

demo.title: Smart Home Controller (Facade)
demo.description: Instead of toggling each switch manually, the Facade provides simple "Macro" buttons that orchestrate everything.
demo.goodMorningDesc: Open curtains, Music on, Lights on
demo.movieNightDesc: Dim lights, TV on, AC on, Close curtains
demo.goodNightDesc: All off, AC on, Lock doors

facade.title: Facade Pattern
facade.description: This pattern provides a simplified interface to a complex system, like a single 'Movie Mode' button that controls lights, TV, and curtains simultaneously.

concept.analogy: In a forest game, each tree has a position (unique) and a texture/model (shared). Instead of loading the texture 1,000 times for 1,000 trees, you load it once and have all 1,000 trees reference that single texture object.
concept.definition: The Flyweight pattern lets you fit more objects into the available amount of RAM by sharing common parts of state between multiple objects instead of keeping all of the data in each object.

usage.point1: Use the Flyweight pattern only when your program must support a huge number of objects which barely fit into available RAM.
usage.point2: Use it when the objects contain duplicate states which can be extracted and shared between multiple objects.

demo.title: Forest Renderer
demo.renderingCapped:
Rendering capped at 2000 (DOM limitation),
but {{count}} objects exist in memory!

flyweight.title: Flyweight Pattern
flyweight.description: This pattern optimizes memory usage by sharing common data among many objects, such as using a single texture for thousands of trees in a forest.

concept.analogy: A credit card is a proxy for a bank account (or cash). You can use it to pay, and the money gets transferred later. It controls access to your funds.
concept.definition: The Proxy pattern lets you provide a substitute or placeholder for another object. A proxy controls access to the original object, allowing you to perform something either before or after the request gets through to the original object.

usage.point1: Lazy initialization (virtual proxy). This is when you have a heavyweight service object that wastes system resources by being always up, even though you only need it from time to time.
usage.point2: Access control (protection proxy). This is when you want only specific clients to be able to use the service object.
usage.point3: Local execution of a remote service (remote proxy). This is when the service object is located on a remote server.
usage.point4: Logging requests (logging proxy). This is when you want to keep a history of requests to the service object.
usage.point5: Caching request results (caching proxy). This is when you need to cache results of client requests and manage the life cycle of this cache.

demo.title: Cached Video Proxy
demo.logCacheHit: Proxy: Cache HIT! Returning saved data for {{id}}.
demo.logCacheMiss: Proxy: Cache MISS. Sending request to RealSubject...
demo.logReceived: Proxy: Received data. Saved to cache.
demo.explainerIdle: Click a button to start a request.
demo.explainerChecking: Proxy checks if data exists in local cache...
demo.explainerFetching: Cache miss! Forwarding request to Real Server (slow)...
demo.explainerReturning: Data found! Returning results to Client.

proxy.title: Proxy Pattern
proxy.description: This pattern acts as a substitute for another object to control access, such as a cache that stores video data to avoid repeated downloads from a slow server.

concept.analogy: It's like calling customer support. First, you get a robot (Handler 1). If it can't help, it passes you to a human agent (Handler 2). If the issue is critical, the agent passes you to a manager (Handler 3).
concept.definition: The Chain of Responsibility pattern lets you pass requests along a chain of handlers. Upon receiving a request, each handler decides either to process the request or to pass it to the next handler in the chain.

demo.title: Support Ticket System
demo.botReply: 🤖 Bot: I can help with "{{request}}". Here is a link to the FAQ.
demo.agentReply: 👨‍💼 Agent: I see you have a complex issue "{{request}}". I'll resolve it manually.
demo.managerReply: 🤵 Manager: Critical issue "{{request}}" escalated to me. Investigating ASAP.

chainOfResponsibility.title: Chain of Responsibility Pattern
chainOfResponsibility.description: This pattern passes a request along a chain of handlers, like a support ticket moving from a bot to an agent and then a manager, until someone resolves it.

concept.analogy: It's like ordering food at a restaurant. You (Client) give an order (Command) to the waiter (Invoker). The waiter doesn't cook; he passes the order to the chef (Receiver). Because the order is an object, it can be queued, modified, or cancelled.
concept.definition: The Command pattern turns a request into a stand-alone object that contains all information about the request. This transformation lets you parameterize methods with different requests, delay or queue a request's execution, and support undoable operations.

command.title: Command Pattern
command.description: This pattern turns a request into a standalone object, allowing you to queue operations or undo actions, like a remote control that remembers your button presses.

concept.analogy: It's rarely used for general-purpose programming languages (too complex) but great for simple domain-specific languages (DSL), like math expressions, SQL parsers, or regular expressions.
concept.definition: The Interpreter pattern is used to define a grammatical representation for a language and an interpreter to interpret the grammar.

usage.point1: Use the Interpreter pattern when your problem can be represented as a sentence in a simple language, and you have to interpret it.
usage.point2: Use it when the grammar is simple and efficiency is not a critical concern.

demo.title: Math Interpreter
demo.label: Enter Expression (space separated)
demo.error: Invalid Expression format. Use space separated: '1 + 2'

interpreter.title: Interpreter Pattern
interpreter.description: This pattern defines a grammar for a language and an interpreter to execute it, useful for parsing mathematical expressions or specific rules.

concept.analogy: It decouples the traversal algorithms from the collection objects. You can have different iterators (Forward, Backward, Shuffle) for the same collection without changing the collection code.
concept.definition: The Iterator pattern lets you traverse elements of a collection without exposing its underlying representation (list, stack, tree, etc.).

usage.point1: Use the Iterator pattern when your collection has a complex data structure under the hood, but you want to hide its complexity from clients (either for convenience or security reasons).
usage.point2: Use the pattern to reduce duplication of the traversal code across your app.
usage.point3: Use the Iterator when you want your code to be able to traverse different data structures or when the types of these structures are unknown beforehand.

iterator.title: Iterator Pattern
iterator.description: This pattern provides a way to access elements of a collection sequentially, like playing through a music playlist, without exposing the underlying list structure.

concept.analogy: Instead of Alice sending a message directly to Bob and Charlie (Many-to-Many dependency), Alice sends it to the ChatRoom (Mediator), and the ChatRoom distributes it. This reduces coupling: components don't need to know about each other, only about the Mediator.
concept.definition: The Mediator pattern restricts direct communications between the objects and forces them to collaborate only via a mediator object.

usage.point1: Use the Mediator pattern when it's hard to change some of the classes because they are tightly coupled to a bunch of other classes.
usage.point2: Use the pattern when you can't reuse a component in a different program because it's too dependent on other components.
usage.point3: Use the Mediator when you find yourself creating tons of component subclasses just to reuse some basic behavior in various contexts.

mediator.title: Mediator Pattern
mediator.description: This pattern centralizes communication between objects, like a chat room handling messages between users so they don't need to connect directly to each other.

concept.analogy: It's commonly used for "Undo" mechanisms. The "Originator" (Editor) creates a "Memento" (Snapshot) containing its state. The "Caretaker" (History List) stores the memento but cannot read/tamper with it.
concept.definition: The Memento pattern lets you save and restore the previous state of an object without revealing the details of its implementation.

usage.point1: Use the Memento pattern when you want to produce snapshots of the object's state to be able to restore a previous state of the object.
usage.point2: Use the pattern when direct access to the object's fields/getters/setters violates its encapsulation.

demo.title: Text Editor (Snapshot)
demo.caretakerDesc: The "Caretaker" (HistoryManager) holds the stack but never modifies the contents.

memento.title: Memento Pattern
memento.description: This pattern captures an object's internal state so it can be restored later, enabling features like undoing text changes in an editor.

concept.analogy: Think of YouTube or a Newsletter. You (the Observer) subscribe to a channel (the Subject). When the channel uploads a new video, it automatically notifies all subscribers. You don't have to check the channel every 5 minutes to see if there's something new.
concept.definition: The Observer pattern defines a subscription mechanism to notify multiple objects about any events that happen to the object they're observing.

usage.point1: Use the Observer pattern when changes to the state of one object may require changing other objects, and the actual set of objects is unknown or changes dynamically.
usage.point2: Use the pattern when some objects in your app must observe others, but only for a limited time or in specific cases.

demo.emptyList: List is empty. Add some fans!

observer.title: Observer Pattern
observer.description: This pattern establishes a subscription mechanism, notifying multiple observers like YouTube subscribers automatically whenever a new event or video occurs.

concept.analogy: Instead of massive switch statements inside a click() method (e.g., if state == playing then pause else if state == stopped then play), you delegate the execution to a state object.
concept.definition: The State pattern lets an object alter its behavior when its internal state changes. It appears as if the object changed its class.

usage.point1: Use the State pattern when you have an object that behaves differently depending on its current state.
usage.point2: Use the pattern when you have a massive switch-case conditional that alters the class behavior according to instance values.

state.title: State Pattern
state.description: This pattern allows an object to change its behavior when its internal state changes, like a music player behaving differently when play is pressed depending on whether it is currently paused or stopped.

concept.analogy: Imagine navigating to the airport. You can choose a Bus strategy, a Taxi strategy, or a Bike strategy. They all accomplish the same goal (getting to the airport), but the algorithm (cost, time, route) is different. The client (traveler) can swap strategies at runtime based on their needs (budget vs speed).
concept.definition: The Strategy pattern defines a family of algorithms, puts each of them into a separate class, and makes their objects interchangeable.

usage.point1: Use the Strategy pattern when you want to use different variants of an algorithm within an object and be able to switch from one algorithm to another during runtime.
usage.point2: Use it when you have a lot of similar classes that only differ in the way they execute some behavior.
usage.point3: Use it to isolate the business logic of a class from the implementation details of algorithms that may not be as important in the context of that logic.

demo.title: Checkout (Context)
demo.redirectPayPal: You will be redirected to PayPal
demo.bankInvoice: Bank Transfer Strategy: Created invoice for {{amount}}. Pending approval.

strategy.title: Strategy Pattern
strategy.description: This pattern enables you to select an algorithm at runtime, such as choosing between Credit Card, PayPal, or Bank Transfer for payment, without changing the checkout logic.

concept.analogy: Think of a recipe. The general steps are "Prep -> Cook -> Serve". The abstract class defines this flow. A PastaDish subclass implements "Boil Water" for Cook. A SteakDish subclass implements "Grill" for Cook. The order remains the same.
concept.definition: The Template Method pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm in the superclass but lets subclasses override specific steps of the algorithm without changing its structure.

usage.point1: Use the Template Method pattern when you want to let clients extend only particular steps of an algorithm, but not the whole algorithm or its structure.
usage.point2: Use the pattern when you have several classes that contain almost identical algorithms with some minor differences.

demo.title: Data Mining Pipeline
demo.pdfParse: PDF: Converting raw text to JSON...

templateMethod.title: Template Method Pattern
templateMethod.description: This pattern defines the skeleton of an algorithm, like a data processing pipeline, allowing subclasses to override specific steps without changing the overall workflow.

concept.analogy: Imagine you have a graph of Shape objects. You want to export them to XML. Instead of adding an exportXML() method to every Shape class (and cluttering them), you create a separate XmlExportVisitor class. The shapes just "accept" the visitor.
concept.definition: The Visitor pattern lets you separate algorithms from the objects on which they operate.

usage.point1: Use the Visitor to clean up the business logic of auxiliary behaviors.
usage.point2: Use the pattern when a behavior makes sense only in some classes of a class hierarchy, but not in others.

visitor.title: Visitor Pattern
visitor.description: This pattern lets you add new operations to existing object structures, such as exporting a group of shapes to XML or JSON, without modifying the shape classes.
